plan.angle: Same structure. Hook: 'In Irkutsk, a lab worker died of pneumonia. Media reported it as suspected pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say the cause is unknown and that no dangerous pathogens were found in her 197 reported contacts. Rospotrebnadzor reported that over 90% had finished monitoring (as of Oct 7, 2026). WHO says the cause is not yet known. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.' Madagascar totals from a single dated WHO report (e.g. 2,348 cases, 202 deaths, 1 Aug–22 Nov 2017, WHO DON 27 Nov 2017), with its confirmed/probable/suspected split. Title: 'How Madagascar Brought Pneumonic Plague Under Control in 2017 (and What It Means Now)'.

plan.why: Evergreen depth piece with a timely hook (Irkutsk contacts finishing monitoring). Few creators cover it in depth, and it backs the calm, expert line that global spread is unlikely. | fact-check: Good evergreen case study, but the status line needs fixing. Verified: on Oct 6, 2026 WHO said Russian authorities told it that no dangerous pathogens were found in any contact, and none had symptoms (UN Geneva newsroom, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier: https://www.unognewsroom.org/story/en/3289/irkutsk-suspected-plague-death-who). Rospotrebnadzor calls the death 'pneumonia of unknown aetiology'. As of Oct 8, WHO (Maria Van Kerkhove) says the cause is still not known (Al Jazeera: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8/russia-dismisses-reports-of-second-plague-case-as-false-information). The '197 contacts' figure is reported by several outlets. The 'over 90% completed monitoring' figure comes from Rospotrebnadzor (it was 60% on Oct 5), so credit Rospotrebnadzor as reported by the outlet, not Euronews alone. I couldn't open a Euronews Oct 7 page that says this; re-check before publishing. Madagascar: WHO DON of 27 Nov 2017 gives 2,348 confirmed, probable and suspected cases and 202 deaths (CFR 8.6%), 1 Aug–22 Nov 2017 (https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/27-november-2017-plague-madagascar-en). WHO AFRO's later update gives 2,384 cases and 207 deaths to 24 Nov. Pick one dated WHO report and don't mix the two. Keep the WHO split of confirmed, probable and suspected cases, which supports section 4. Don't mention the unverified second-case media reports, which the Kremlin calls false and WHO is asking about, beyond 'WHO has asked Russia for more information'. 'Stopped' is acceptable if you cite WHO's end-of-outbreak statement. Otherwise say 'brought under control'.

package.description:
How did Madagascar bring its 2017 pneumonic plague outbreak under control? WHO reports describe the 3 tools in this video: contact tracing, preventive antibiotics given by health authorities, and fast care in dedicated treatment centres.

Quick answer: WHO counted 2,348 confirmed, probable and suspected plague cases and 202 deaths (1 Aug–22 Nov 2017). By late November, 7,289 contacts had been identified and all had completed preventive antibiotics. Irkutsk, as of Oct 8, 2026: WHO says the cause of the reported death is still not known. On Oct 6, WHO said Russian authorities found no dangerous pathogens in any contact and none had symptoms. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.

This video is general information, not medical advice. If you think you've been exposed, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Don't self-treat. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
WHO, Plague – Madagascar (Disease Outbreak News, 27 Nov 2017): https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/27-november-2017-plague-madagascar-en
UN News, Testing and monitoring underway in suspected Russia plague death (2026): https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168533
CDC, How Plague Spreads: https://www.cdc.gov/plague/causes/index.html
Randremanana R et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2019: https://doi.org/10.1016/S1473-3099(18)30730-8

package.pinned_comment: In Madagascar's 2017 outbreak, WHO counted 2,348 confirmed, probable and suspected cases. Of the 1,791 pneumonic cases, WHO's November report classed about 1 in 5 as lab-confirmed. A later peer-reviewed analysis using final classifications found 32 of 1,878 notified pneumonic cases (about 2%) confirmed. So for every outbreak number, including Irkutsk (cause not yet known, as of Oct 8, 2026), ask: confirmed, probable or suspected, and as of when? General information, not medical advice. Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

script.working_title: How Madagascar Brought Pneumonic Plague Under Control in 2017 (and What It Means Now)
script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity (dated news decoder: Irkutsk status as of Oct 8, 2026) leading into an open loop (the easy-to-misread number inside Madagascar's 2,348 cases, paid off near the end)

scenes.narration: In Irkutsk, Russia, a laboratory worker died of a severe pneumonia. Media reported it as suspected pneumonic plague.

visual.stock_query: calm newsroom desk with Siberia map

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: breaking-news open with a dated, hedged status

scenes.narration: Russian authorities describe the death as pneumonia of unknown cause. And as of October 8, 2026, WHO says the cause is still not known.

visual.stock_query: doctor with clipboard and question mark

scenes.retention_device: Curiosity gap: official answer still pending

scenes.narration: On October 6, WHO said Russian authorities told it that no dangerous pathogens were found in any contact, and that none had symptoms. As of October 5, media reported nearly 200 people isolated or under observation.

visual.stock_query: group of people with calm health workers

scenes.narration: So right now, plague is not confirmed. But not confirmed isn't the same as ruled out. WHO has asked Russia for more information.
scenes.retention_device: Myth correction that sets up the video's reading habit

scenes.narration: Which raises a bigger question. When pneumonic plague really does spread between people, in a big city, what actually brings it under control?
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer that frames the whole video

scenes.narration: In 2017, Madagascar found out. WHO's November report counted 2,348 confirmed, probable and suspected plague cases, including 202 deaths, between August 1 and November 22.
scenes.retention_device: Proof point: real-world scale with a dated source

scenes.narration: Yet in that same report, WHO said no new confirmed pneumonic cases had been notified since November 14. No new miracle drug. Just old antibiotics used fast, and a lot of legwork.
scenes.retention_device: But/therefore turn: big outbreak, ordinary solution

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you'll know the 3 tools that did it. And there's one number inside that 2,348 that's easy to misread. It changes how you read every outbreak headline, including this one.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop planted (pays off in 'The number people misread')

scenes.narration: First, a quick refresher. Plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, which circulates in small mammals like rodents, and in their fleas.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a fast primer promise

scenes.narration: Most people who get plague get it from an infected flea bite. That usually causes bubonic plague, with painful, swollen lymph nodes.

visual.stock_query: cartoon flea hopping off a rodent

scenes.narration: If the bacteria reach the bloodstream, that's septicemic plague. If they reach the lungs, it's pneumonic plague.
And here's the difference that matters. CDC says pneumonic plague is the only form that can spread from person to person, through respiratory droplets.
scenes.retention_device: Key-fact emphasis: 'here's the difference that matters'

scenes.narration: CDC says that spread requires direct and close contact with someone who has pneumonic plague. Keep that phrase in mind, because the whole Madagascar response was built around it.

visual.stock_query: two chairs close together, others far

scenes.retention_device: Seed for later payoff (contact tracing logic)

scenes.narration: WHO also says pneumonic plague's incubation can be as short as 24 hours. So someone who feels fine today could be ill tomorrow.
scenes.retention_device: Urgency stake that explains the speed of the response

scenes.narration: How dangerous is it? WHO says plague is most severe in its septicemic and pneumonic forms, with a death rate of 30 to 100% if left untreated.

visual.stat_label: Untreated death rate, septicemic and pneumonic (WHO)

scenes.retention_device: Shock stat, immediately balanced in next scene

scenes.narration: But here's the hopeful part. For pneumonic plague, WHO says recovery rates are high if it's detected and treated within 24 hours of symptoms starting.
Hold onto that 24-hour window. Madagascar's whole strategy was a race against it.

visual.stock_query: health workers racing a giant clock

scenes.narration: Plague wasn't new to Madagascar. In 2017, WHO said the country reports around 400 cases a year, mainly bubonic.

visual.stock_query: Madagascar map with calm highland hills

scenes.narration: But 2017 broke the pattern. WHO said this outbreak started earlier than the usual plague season, and it was affecting large urban areas.
Those included the capital, Antananarivo, and the port city of Toamasina. A later peer-reviewed outbreak report called it an urban plague epidemic.

visual.stock_query: two city pins on Madagascar map

scenes.retention_device: Concrete place names make it vivid

scenes.narration: And this time, most cases were pneumonic. Of the 2,348 cases in WHO's November report, 1,791, about 3 in 4, were classified as pneumonic plague.
Why does that matter? A bubonic case doesn't pass from person to person unless the infection reaches the lungs. A pneumonic case in a crowded city can, with close contact.
How did it reach the cities? The first identified patient was a man who fell ill while travelling by shared taxi from the central highlands toward the east coast, and died on the way.
scenes.retention_device: Micro-story about the first identified patient

scenes.narration: From there, chains of person-to-person spread followed, which is exactly what pneumonic plague can do with close contact.
So here's the puzzle. The one form of plague that can spread between people, in two big cities. Why didn't it just keep growing?
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: open question before the 3 tools

scenes.narration: The first tool is the least glamorous one: contact tracing.

visual.stock_query: magnifying glass over a contact list

scenes.retention_device: Payoff begins: first of three tools revealed

scenes.narration: The logic is simple. CDC says person-to-person spread of pneumonic plague requires direct and close contact with someone who's ill. So if you find everyone who had that contact, you can get ahead of the next case.

visual.stock_query: health worker drawing a contact web

scenes.retention_device: Callback to the 'close contact' phrase planted earlier

scenes.narration: In Madagascar, teams identified the contacts of cases and followed them up. WHO reported 7,289 contacts identified by late November 2017, and all had completed preventive antibiotics.

visual.stat_label: Contacts identified, all completed preventive antibiotics

scenes.retention_device: Scale detail with a hard number

scenes.narration: Follow-up means checking on each person and watching for fever or cough, so anyone who gets sick is found and treated fast, ideally inside that 24-hour window.
Think of it like smoke detectors in every room next to a fire. You don't wait to see flames. You watch the rooms the fire could reach.
Every contact found early is a chain of transmission that may never get started.
Contact monitoring is the same basic approach being used in Irkutsk. As of October 6, WHO said Russian authorities reported that none of the contacts had symptoms.
scenes.retention_device: Link back to the news hook

scenes.narration: But with a germ this fast, watching alone isn't enough. Madagascar added a second layer, and it's the one people most often get wrong.
Tool two: preventive antibiotics, given by health authorities.
Because plague is bacterial, common antibiotics can treat it, especially when they're started early.

And CDC guidance says preventive antibiotics should be considered for people who had close, sustained contact with someone with pneumonic plague without adequate protective equipment. A clinician or health authority makes that call.
On October 6, 2017, WHO said it had delivered nearly 1.2 million doses of antibiotics to Madagascar, and released 1.5 million US dollars in emergency funds.
WHO said those supplies could treat up to 5,000 patients and protect up to 100,000 people who might be exposed.
Notice how this worked. Health authorities decided who needed antibiotics, based on who had been in contact. Not stockpiles at home.

visual.stock_query: official health team at a table

scenes.retention_device: 'Notice' pattern draws attention to the key nuance

scenes.narration: So if you've heard you should stockpile antibiotics just in case, that's not how outbreaks are controlled. Which drug, for whom, and for how long is a clinical decision. If you think you've been exposed, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.

visual.myth: Keep antibiotics at home, just in case
visual.fact: Clinicians and health authorities decide who needs preventive antibiotics

scenes.retention_device: Myth attack on a belief viewers may hold

scenes.narration: Contacts covered. But what about the people who were already sick? That's where the 24-hour clock comes back.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook and callback to the 24-hour loop

scenes.narration: Tool three: fast treatment, in dedicated centres.
WHO reported that partners helped set up plague treatment centres in Madagascar. Centres like these let patients get care quickly, away from their households.
That does two jobs at once. The patient gets antibiotics quickly, and the droplets that could infect family members stay away from the family.
Testing mattered too. The Institut Pasteur de Madagascar's plague laboratory handled laboratory confirmation.
Now look at the outcome. WHO's November report gave a case fatality rate of 8.6%: 202 deaths among all reported cases.
WHO judged the risk moderate within Madagascar, and low at regional and global levels. Nine countries and territories with travel and trade links were made priorities for plague preparedness.
Compare 8.6% with WHO's 30 to 100% for untreated severe plague. The gap is striking. But 8.6% hides a catch, and it's the number I promised you.
scenes.retention_device: 'But here's where it gets weird' re-hook into the main payoff

scenes.narration: Remember that total of 2,348 cases? Here's the twist.
Those weren't 2,348 lab-confirmed plague infections. WHO's count combined 3 categories: confirmed, probable and suspected.
Of the 1,791 pneumonic cases, WHO's November report classed 22% as confirmed, 34% as probable and 44% as suspected.
So in WHO's November count, about 1 in 5 pneumonic cases was lab-confirmed, and more than 4 in 10 were suspected.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising stat, with a sharper one coming next

scenes.narration: But a later peer-reviewed analysis, using final classifications, found even fewer: 32 of 1,878 notified pneumonic cases, about 2%, were confirmed, and 386, about 21%, were probable.
scenes.retention_device: Most surprising stat saved for last

scenes.narration: A suspected case is someone whose symptoms and circumstances fit the case definition. During an outbreak, people with other respiratory illnesses can fit that definition too, which is why lab confirmation matters.

visual.stock_query: queue of people at clinic door

scenes.narration: That's the point of a wide net. It can catch real cases early, inside the 24-hour window. The trade-off is that the headline number looks bigger than the confirmed one.
It also affects the death rate. The 8.6% was calculated across all categories, so it isn't a clean measure of plague alone.
So here's the habit to take away. With any outbreak number, ask: confirmed, probable or suspected, and as of when?
scenes.retention_device: Main loop payoff turned into a reusable habit

scenes.narration: So what does Madagascar tell us about Irkutsk?

visual.stock_query: two map pins joined by a line

scenes.retention_device: New loop: apply the lesson to the news

scenes.narration: First, scale. Madagascar had thousands of reported cases across crowded cities. In Irkutsk, what's been reported is one death, with the cause not yet known, and, as of October 5, nearly 200 people under observation.
Second, the tools are the same: tracing contacts, preventive antibiotics when health authorities judge they're needed, and fast treatment for anyone who falls ill.

visual.stock_query: three tool icons on a shelf

scenes.narration: Third, the signals so far. As of October 6, WHO said Russian authorities reported no dangerous pathogens in any contact, and no symptoms.
Still, the honest status is: cause not yet known, with WHO seeking more information. Not confirmed isn't ruled out, so we'll keep dating every update.
scenes.on_screen_text: Oct 8 status: cause not yet known

scenes.narration: And if plague were ever confirmed there, Madagascar shows that a far larger pneumonic outbreak was brought under control with tools that already exist.
scenes.retention_device: Reassuring payoff of the opening question

scenes.narration: Here's your practical checklist.

Person-to-person spread of pneumonic plague needs direct, close contact. Antibiotics work best when started early. Preventive antibiotics for contacts are decided by clinicians or health authorities. And every number deserves the question: confirmed or suspected?

visual.stock_query: four sticky notes on a board

scenes.narration: If you've possibly been exposed, say close contact with someone who has suspected pneumonic plague, or time in an area where plague occurs, know the warning signs.
CDC lists fever, headache and weakness, with a rapidly developing pneumonia: shortness of breath, chest pain and cough.
With possible exposure and those symptoms, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Don't self-treat, and don't wait it out.
For status updates, go to official sources like WHO and national health authorities, not screenshots or rumours.
And if you're worried, talk to a health professional. That's exactly what they're there for.
Next, we're going inside high-containment labs: how they keep dangerous bacteria in, and what happens after a lab exposure. Subscribe so you catch it, with every status update dated.
scenes.retention_device: Forward open loop tied to the next benefit

factcheck.summary:
I checked all 11 sources and they all exist. The Madagascar figures match WHO's 27 November 2017 outbreak report: 2,348 cases, 202 deaths, a death rate of 8.6% across all reported cases, and 1,791 pneumonic cases. Of those, 22% were confirmed, 34% probable and 44% suspected. The report also gives 7,289 contacts who all completed preventive antibiotics, no new confirmed pneumonic cases after 14 November, and a risk rating of moderate within Madagascar and low at regional and global levels, with nine priority countries and territories. WHO's 6 October 2017 release confirms about 1.2 million doses (1,190,000), US$1.5 million in emergency funds, and supplies to treat up to 5,000 patients and protect up to 100,000 people. The Lancet Infectious Diseases 2019 paper confirms 32 of 1,878 pneumonic cases confirmed (2%), 386 probable (21%), and the first patient who died travelling by bush taxi from the Central Highlands toward Toamasina.

The WHO fact sheet (updated 29 September 2026) supports incubation as short as 24 hours, a 30–100% death rate if untreated, and high recovery when treated within 24 hours of symptoms. CDC's pages match the script's wording: pneumonic is the only form that spreads between people, spread requires direct and close contact, and the symptom list is complete. CDC's guidance says preventive antibiotics "should be considered" for close, sustained contact without adequate protective equipment, which the script reflects.

The Irkutsk status matches the sources. On 6 October 2026, WHO via UN Geneva said Russia reported no dangerous pathogens in any contact and no symptoms, and that no cause of death has been officially confirmed. On 8 October, Russia described it as "pneumonia of unknown aetiology" and WHO said it doesn't know the cause and wants information (Al Jazeera). Outlook India reported nearly 200 contacts on 5 October. A tracker site claims Russia told WHO there was "no plague in her or anyone else" and released all contacts. I couldn't confirm that in any WHO or UN source, so the script is right to leave it out.

The script handles framing and safety well: it dates every status, says not confirmed isn't ruled out, explains that 8.6% includes suspected cases, carries the no-self-treatment and no-stockpiling message, and includes the urgent-care and talk-to-a-health-professional lines. Only minor wording fixes remain. Re-check the Irkutsk status against WHO and Russian official sources at publish time.

issues.claim: Pneumonic plague spreads only through close contact with someone who's ill.
issues.problem: This widens the claim beyond CDC's wording. CDC is talking about spread between people, and says it needs direct and close contact with the person or animal that has pneumonic plague. For example, people can catch it from infected cats.
issues.fix: The logic is simple. CDC says person-to-person spread of pneumonic plague requires direct and close contact with someone who's ill. So if you find everyone who had that contact, you can get ahead of the next case.

issues.claim: WHO reported that Madagascar's response included plague treatment centres, where patients could be cared for and kept apart from others.
issues.problem: WHO's report says IFRC, UNICEF and USAID supported case management, including setting up plague treatment centres. It doesn't explicitly say the centres were for isolation. 'Kept apart from others' is our own inference, but the sentence credits it to WHO.
issues.fix: WHO reported that partners helped set up plague treatment centres in Madagascar. Centres like these let patients get care quickly, away from their households.

issues.claim: During a frightening outbreak, people with ordinary chest infections can fit that definition too.
issues.problem: This is reasonable, but the sources don't say it directly. Hedge it so it reads as an explanation, not a sourced finding.
issues.fix: A suspected case is someone whose symptoms and circumstances fit the case definition. During an outbreak, people with other respiratory illnesses can fit that definition too, which is why lab confirmation matters.

issues.claim: Media reported it as suspected pneumonic plague.
issues.problem: The scene cites S8 and S9. The media report is best supported by S11 (Outlook India, 5 Oct 2026), which this scene doesn't cite.

audio.soundNotes: Music is already close to target (-13.5 dB under voice, -13.2 in pauses); a small -0.7 dB trim keeps it from ever crowding the narrator while still swelling nicely in the pauses. The big fixes are a handful of cues that measured far louder than the voice during speech (a bubble at -5.1 dB, a pop at -3.9 dB, blips at -5 to -7 dB, several swooshes at -7 to -10 dB) — these have been pulled down into the -14 to -20 dB "felt" zone. I also thinned the dense 606-607s cluster (6 overlapping swooshes/ding in under a second) down to 3 and trimmed a redundant blip in the 517-519s burst. Added five bespoke story-moment sounds (news-alert throb on the cold open, a tense heartbeat on "race against 24h," taxi-interior ambience for the shared-taxi exposure story, a quiet hospital-corridor bed for the treatment-centres section, and a calm resolving chime into the outro/teaser) to add texture the stock kit can't give without ever competing with the voice.

issues: mascot smile may read as slightly too cheerful for an outbreak topic, but shield/safety framing stays reassuring not trivializing

'Early wins' + plague-vs-antibiotics doesn't visually tie to Madagascar or the 'how did they stop it' narrative as tightly as #0; reads as a generic treatment message more than an outbreak-response story

'The misread number' curiosity gap doesn't match the title's promise ('how did Madagascar stop the outbreak') and risks feeling like a bait-and-switch/clickbait tangent since title never mentions a number to misread

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are fully legible at phone size with clean, uncluttered text (≤2 lines, large bold type, no cropping). #0 ('3 TOOLS') most directly pays off the title's explicit 'How did...stop it?' question with a concrete, countable promise, which the playbook's data favors (specific, concrete hooks over vague teases). The friendly shield mascot keeps it reassuring rather than alarmist, in line with brand tone. #1 ('EARLY WINS' vs plague/antibiotics) is clear and emotionally resolves well, but it frames a general treatment-works message rather than the Madagascar outbreak-response story the title promises, making it a slightly weaker match to the curiosity gap set up by the title. #2 ('THE MISREAD NUMBER') has the strongest curiosity gap in isolation, but it doesn't connect to the title's actual question about stopping the outbreak — a viewer could feel the thumbnail oversells an unrelated angle, bordering on a mismatch between title and thumbnail promise. Given equal legibility, #0 offers the best combination of relevance, specificity and honest curiosity pull.

issues.claim: A later peer-reviewed analysis using final classifications found about 2% confirmed.
